canonicalExplanation.summary: A **union** is like a struct whose members **share the same memory**: it's as big as its largest member, and holds **one** of them at a time. Writing `u.d = 2.5` overwrites whatever `u.i` held. The union **doesn't remember** which member is active, so reading the wrong one gives meaningless bits. The safe pattern is a **tagged union**: a struct holding an **enum tag** that records which member is active, next to the union. Set the tag whenever you write, and check it (with a switch) before every read.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A settings parser stores each value in `union { int i; double d; } v;`. A setting saved as the double 2.5 is later read with v.i and shows 0, or some huge number, depending on the machine. A tagged value stores an enum kind beside a union and reads integer or floating member only when the tag names that member. In this lesson you'll implement and safely inspect a simple tagged union.

```predict
{"question": "You write u.d = 2.5, then read u.i. What do you get?", "options": ["2", "Meaningless bits: the union doesn't convert or track the active member"], "answer": 1, "why": "The tag is how your code knows which member is valid."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **One-dimensional arrays**, **Addresses and dereference**, **Structures** and **Enumerations** (exhaustive switches).

sections.heading: The model: shared storage plus a tag
Keep tag and data together

includes: Explain shared storage in unions and why they don't track the active member.
Build tagged unions with an enum tag, constructors and a switch before every read.

outcomes: Implement and safely inspect a simple tagged union.

examples.title: A value that is an int or a double
examples.situation: A tagged value stores an enum kind beside a union and reads integer or floating member only when the tag names that member.
walkthrough: **A tagged value stores an enum kind beside a union:** struct Value holds kind and as.
**Constructors set both:** make_double(2.5) sets kind to KIND_DOUBLE and as.d to 2.5.
**Reads integer or floating member only when the tag names that member:** print_value switches on kind, so 2.5 will print as a double.
examples.result: Settings read back exactly as they were stored.

examples.title: Adding a string kind
examples.situation: The parser must now also store short text values.
walkthrough: Add KIND_TEXT to enum Kind and char text[16] to the union.
Add make_text with a bounded copy.
-Wswitch flags print_value until the new case is handled.
examples.result: The new kind is supported everywhere, with the compiler pointing at each place.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: A union remembers which member was last written and prevents code from reading the wrong alternative.
misconceptions.correction: A union is just shared storage with no record of the active member. Your code must track it with a tag and check before reading.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did 2.5 read back as nonsense?

analogy.example: A union is like **a single parking space** that can hold a car or a motorbike, but not both. The space doesn't know which is parked there; the **ticket on the windscreen** (the tag) tells you. Don't try to drive the car out if the ticket says motorbike.
limitations: You can see vehicles; you can't see which union member is active.
Updating the vehicle means updating the ticket too.

steps.explanation: The tagged value stores an enum kind beside the union.
The code reads the tag before touching any member.
It reads the floating member only when the tag names that member.

trace.textAlternative: Tracing a tagged union. Step 1, Store: kind is KIND_DOUBLE; as.d is 2.5. The tagged value stores an enum kind beside the union. Step 2, Check: switch is KIND_DOUBLE case. The code reads the tag before touching any member. Step 3, Read: output is double 2.50. It reads the floating member only when the tag names that member.

nearTransfer.prompt: Add a bool kind to struct Value with make_bool and printing. Print sizeof(struct Value) before and after, and explain why it barely changes.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a tiny shape system: struct Shape with enum ShapeKind {CIRCLE, RECT} and a union of {radius} and {width, height}. Implement area() with a switch and test both shapes plus an invalid kind.
scaffold: Return -1 or false for invalid kind.

remediation.explanation: For every union read ask: **what does the tag say, and am I reading that member?** Create values only through functions that set tag and data together.
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "Adding a string kind".

recap.summary: To implement tagged unions, remember union members share storage and the union doesn't track which one is active, so pair it with an enum tag in a struct, create values through constructors that set both, and switch on the tag before reading any member.
